content: Airway infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) lead to progressive lung damage, and oxidative stress has been implicated as a contributing factor in this process. Supplementation with antioxidant micronutrients, such as vitamin E, vitamin C, beta-carotene, selenium, or N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which serves as a precursor to glutathione, may help maintain a balance between oxidants and antioxidants. Glutathione or NAC can also be administered via inhalation, which not only provides antioxidant effects but also has a mucolytic action. Current research suggests a link between oxidative stress and lung function in CF patients. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of antioxidants, including vitamin C, vitamin E, beta-carotene, selenium, and glutathione (or NAC as its precursor), on lung function, inflammation, and oxidative stress markers in individuals with CF. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing these antioxidants, either individually or in combination, to placebo or standard care in CF patients. The studies were assessed for bias, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. A total of 20 studies involving 924 participants (children and adults) were included. Sixteen studies (639 participants) investigated oral antioxidant supplementation, while four studies (285 participants) examined inhaled supplements. Only one study was deemed free of bias. For oral supplementation, the effect of NAC on lung function, measured as the change in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) % predicted, was uncertain at three months due to very low-quality evidence. However, at six months, moderate-quality evidence suggested that NAC likely improved FEV1% predicted, with a mean difference (MD) of 4.38%. A study on combined vitamin and selenium supplementation reported a greater decline in FEV1% predicted in the control group at two months. Regarding quality of life (QoL), one study found that NAC likely had little to no effect at six months, while another study reported a small improvement in QoL favoring the control group at two months. NAC also likely had no significant effect on body mass index (BMI) at six months. A study on mixed vitamin and mineral supplementation suggested a slightly lower risk of pulmonary exacerbations at six months compared to multivitamin supplementation, though the evidence was of low quality. Adverse events were reported in nine studies, but no consistent differences were observed between treatment and control groups. Studies on beta-carotene and vitamin E consistently showed increased plasma levels of these antioxidants. For inhaled supplementation, two studies indicated that inhaled glutathione likely improved FEV1% predicted at three months but not at six months. These studies also reported improvements in absolute FEV1 (in liters) at both three and six months. Inhaled glutathione likely had little to no effect on QoL at six months. No significant changes in BMI were observed at two or 12 months in the limited studies that reported this outcome. One study found no difference in the time to the first pulmonary exacerbation at six months. Adverse events were similar between treatment and control groups, with low-quality evidence. The authors concluded that antioxidant micronutrients do not appear to have a significant positive effect on clinical outcomes in CF. However, oral glutathione supplementation showed some benefits for lung function and oxidative stress reduction. Inhaled and oral glutathione appeared to improve lung function, but the overall impact of antioxidants in CF remains difficult to assess due to the complexity of concurrent treatments, such as intensive antibiotic regimens. Further research is needed, particularly in young children, using advanced outcome measures like lung clearance index and bronchiectasis scores from chest imaging. Future studies should also focus on optimizing study design variables, such as dosage and timing, and clarifying the biological mechanisms of oxidative stress in CF. Additionally, the potential benefits of antioxidants in CF patients receiving CFTR modulator therapies should be explored.
